## Variance {#sec-variance}

```{r}
#| label: setup-2-4
#| include: false
source(if (file.exists("R/setup.R")) "R/setup.R" else "../R/setup.R")
```

### Learning Objectives

1. Explain why the variance matters in economics (risk, volatility, price stability).
2. Read the chi-square table (Table 6).
3. Construct and interpret a confidence interval for $\sigma^2$ and $\sigma$.
4. Carry out a chi-square test for $\sigma^2$ in five steps.

### Concept

The mean tells us the typical value; the variance tells us how much values
**vary**. In finance the standard deviation of returns is the most common
measure of **risk** (volatility). A central bank cares about the stability of
prices, and a firm cares about the stability of its sales.

To make inferences about $\sigma^2$ we use the sample variance $s^2$. If the
population is normal,
$$
\chi^2 = \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma^2}
$$
follows a **chi-square distribution** with $n-1$ degrees of freedom. The
chi-square distribution takes only positive values and is skewed to the right.

```{r}
#| label: fig-chisq-shape
#| fig-cap: "Chi-square distributions are skewed to the right; the skew decreases as df increases"
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center
cs <- data.frame(x = rep(seq(0.01, 40, length.out = 400), 3),
                 df = rep(c("df = 4", "df = 10", "df = 20"), each = 400))
cs$y <- dchisq(cs$x, as.numeric(sub("df = ", "", cs$df)))
cs$df <- factor(cs$df, levels = c("df = 4", "df = 10", "df = 20"))
ggplot(cs, aes(x, y, linetype = df)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, linetype = NULL) + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## The population must be normal

The chi-square methods for a variance are sensitive to non-normality, even for
large samples. Use them only when the data are approximately normal.
:::

### Reading the Chi-Square Table

Table 6 gives $\chi^2$ values with a stated area to the left, for df = 1 to 100.
The curve is **not symmetric**, so for a two-sided test or a CI we read two
different values from the table; we cannot use a minus sign.

**Example 2.4.1.** For df = 23, find $\chi^2_{0.025,\,23}$, $\chi^2_{0.975,\,23}$ and $\chi^2_{0.95,\,23}$.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

Row df = 23: $\chi^2_{0.025,\,23} = `r crit_chisq(.025, 23)`$,
$\chi^2_{0.975,\,23} = `r crit_chisq(.975, 23)`$ and
$\chi^2_{0.95,\,23} = `r crit_chisq(.95, 23)`$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-chisq-23
#| fig-cap: "Areas 0.025 in each tail of the chi-square distribution with df = 23"
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center
crit_plot("chisq", "two", df1 = 23)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}

#| label: fig-yt-2-4-1

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 2.4.1"}
(a) $\chi^2_{0.05,\,19} = `r crit_chisq(.05, 19)`$

(b) $\chi^2_{0.995,\,10} = `r crit_chisq(.995, 10)`$

(c) $\chi^2_{0.025,\,30} = `r crit_chisq(.025, 30)`$
:::

### Formulas and Conditions

**Condition:** a random sample from a normal population.

**$(1-\alpha)100\%$ confidence interval for $\sigma^2$**
$$
\left(\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}},\;
      \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}}\right)
$$
Take the square root of both limits to get a CI for $\sigma$. The larger
chi-square value gives the **lower** limit. The interval is not symmetric
about $s^2$.

**Test statistic** for $H_0: \sigma^2 = \sigma_0^2$, with df $= n-1$
$$
\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}
$$

| $H_1$ | Critical region |
|:---:|:---|
| $\sigma^2 \ne \sigma_0^2$ | $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} < \chi^2_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}$ or $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} > \chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}$ |
| $\sigma^2 < \sigma_0^2$ | $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} < \chi^2_{\alpha,\,n-1}$ |
| $\sigma^2 > \sigma_0^2$ | $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} > \chi^2_{1-\alpha,\,n-1}$ |

A claim about $\sigma$ is tested as the same claim about $\sigma^2$: for
example $\sigma > 2$ is $\sigma^2 > 4$.

```{r}
#| label: ex-2-4
a_n <- 24; a_df <- a_n - 1; a_s <- 2.6; a_sig0 <- 2
a_ss <- a_df * a_s^2
a_chi <- round(a_ss / a_sig0^2, 3)
a_lo_c <- crit_chisq(.025, a_df); a_hi_c <- crit_chisq(.975, a_df); a_95 <- crit_chisq(.95, a_df)
a_v_lo <- round(a_ss / a_hi_c, 4); a_v_hi <- round(a_ss / a_lo_c, 4)
```

### Example

**Example 2.4.2.** A fund manager states that the standard deviation of
the fund's monthly return is 2%. An investor suspects the fund is riskier. Over
the last `r a_n` months the standard deviation of the monthly return was
$s$ = `r a_s`%. Assume monthly returns are normally distributed.

(a) Construct a 95% confidence interval for the variance and the standard deviation of the monthly return.
(b) At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether the standard deviation is more than 2%.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

$s^2 = `r a_s`^2 = `r num(a_s^2)`$, df = `r a_df`, $(n-1)s^2 = `r a_df`(`r num(a_s^2)`) = `r num(a_ss)`$.

**(a)** $\chi^2_{0.025,\,`r a_df`} = `r a_lo_c`$ and $\chi^2_{0.975,\,`r a_df`} = `r a_hi_c`$.
$$
\left(\frac{`r num(a_ss)`}{`r a_hi_c`},\; \frac{`r num(a_ss)`}{`r a_lo_c`}\right)
= (`r fmt(a_v_lo, 4)`,\; `r fmt(a_v_hi, 4)`)
$$
For $\sigma$: $(\sqrt{`r fmt(a_v_lo, 4)`},\ \sqrt{`r fmt(a_v_hi, 4)`}) = (`r fmt(sqrt(a_v_lo), 4)`,\ `r fmt(sqrt(a_v_hi), 4)`)$

We are 95% confident that the standard deviation of the fund's monthly return
is between `r fmt(sqrt(a_v_lo), 4)`% and `r fmt(sqrt(a_v_hi), 4)`%.
Note that $s$ = `r a_s` is not in the middle of the interval.

**(b)**

**Step 1: Hypotheses.** $H_0: \sigma^2 = `r a_sig0^2`$ $\quad H_1: \sigma^2 > `r a_sig0^2`$ (that is, $\sigma > `r a_sig0`$)

**Step 2: Level of significance.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3: Test statistic.**
$$
\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2} = \frac{`r num(a_ss)`}{`r a_sig0^2`} = `r fmt(a_chi, 3)`
$$

**Step 4: Critical value and critical region.** df = `r a_df`:
$\chi^2_{0.95,\,`r a_df`} = `r a_95`$. Critical region: $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} > `r a_95`$.

**Step 5: Decision and interpretation.**
$\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(a_chi, 3)`$ falls in the critical region
($`r fmt(a_chi, 3)` > `r a_95`$), so we reject $H_0$.
That is, the standard deviation of the fund's monthly return is more than 2% at
the 0.05 level of significance.
:::

```{r}
#| label: yt-2-4
b_n <- 20; b_df <- b_n - 1; b_s <- 4.5; b_sig0 <- 3
b_ss <- b_df * b_s^2; b_chi <- round(b_ss / b_sig0^2, 3)
b_lo_c <- crit_chisq(.025, b_df); b_hi_c <- crit_chisq(.975, b_df)
b_v_lo <- round(b_ss / b_hi_c, 4); b_v_hi <- round(b_ss / b_lo_c, 4)
```

### Your Turn

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 2.4.2

A price-stabilization policy aims to keep the standard deviation of the weekly
retail price of pork at 3 baht per kg. Over `r b_n` weeks the standard deviation
was $s$ = `r b_s` baht. Assume prices are normally distributed.

(a) Construct a 95% confidence interval for $\sigma$.
(b) At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether the standard deviation is different from 3 baht.
:::

::: {.workspace lines="4"}
:::

::: {.workspace steps="names"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 2.4.2"}
$s^2 = `r num(b_s^2)`$, df = `r b_df`, $(n-1)s^2 = `r num(b_ss)`$;
$\chi^2_{0.025,\,`r b_df`} = `r b_lo_c`$, $\chi^2_{0.975,\,`r b_df`} = `r b_hi_c`$.

**(a)** CI for $\sigma^2$: $(`r num(b_ss)`/`r b_hi_c`,\ `r num(b_ss)`/`r b_lo_c`) = (`r fmt(b_v_lo, 4)`,\ `r fmt(b_v_hi, 4)`)$.
CI for $\sigma$: (`r fmt(sqrt(b_v_lo), 4)`, `r fmt(sqrt(b_v_hi), 4)`). We are 95%
confident that the standard deviation of the weekly pork price is between
`r fmt(sqrt(b_v_lo), 4)` and `r fmt(sqrt(b_v_hi), 4)` baht.

**(b)**

**Step 1.** $H_0: \sigma^2 = `r b_sig0^2` \quad H_1: \sigma^2 \ne `r b_sig0^2`$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = `r num(b_ss)`/`r b_sig0^2` = `r fmt(b_chi, 3)`$

**Step 4.** Critical region: $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} < `r b_lo_c`$ or $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} > `r b_hi_c`$.

**Step 5.** $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(b_chi, 3)`$ falls in the critical region
($`r fmt(b_chi, 3)` > `r b_hi_c`$), so we reject $H_0$.
That is, the standard deviation of the weekly pork price is different from 3
baht at the 0.05 level of significance; since $s$ = `r b_s`, it is higher than
3 baht, so the policy target was not met.
:::

### Formula Summary

| | Formula |
|:---|:---|
| Condition | population normal |
| $(1-\alpha)100\%$ CI for $\sigma^2$ | $\left(\dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}},\ \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}}\right)$; square root for $\sigma$ |
| Test statistic | $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}$, df $= n-1$ |
| Critical region | $\ne$: $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} < \chi^2_{\alpha/2}$ or $> \chi^2_{1-\alpha/2}$; $<$: $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} < \chi^2_{\alpha}$; $>$: $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} > \chi^2_{1-\alpha}$ |

```{r}
#| label: ex-2-4-exercises
e1_n <- 16; e1_df <- 15; e1_s <- 7.2; e1_sig0 <- 10
e1_ss <- e1_df * e1_s^2; e1_chi <- round(e1_ss / e1_sig0^2, 3); e1_c <- crit_chisq(.05, e1_df)
e2_n <- 25; e2_df <- 24; e2_s <- 0.35
e2_ss <- e2_df * e2_s^2; e2_lo_c <- crit_chisq(.05, e2_df); e2_hi_c <- crit_chisq(.95, e2_df)
e2_v_lo <- round(e2_ss / e2_hi_c, 4); e2_v_hi <- round(e2_ss / e2_lo_c, 4)
```

### Exercises

**2.4.1** Before a new ordering system, the standard deviation of a shop's daily
sales was 10 units. After the system was introduced, `r e1_n` days of sales had
a standard deviation of `r e1_s` units. At
$\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether the standard deviation is now less than 10 units.
Assume normality.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 2.4.1"}
**Step 1.** $H_0: \sigma^2 = 100 \quad H_1: \sigma^2 < 100$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = `r e1_df`(`r num(e1_s^2)`)/100 = `r fmt(e1_chi, 3)`$

**Step 4.** $\chi^2_{0.05,\,`r e1_df`} = `r e1_c`$. Critical region: $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} < `r e1_c`$.

**Step 5.** $\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(e1_chi, 3)`$ does not fall in the critical
region ($`r fmt(e1_chi, 3)` > `r e1_c`$), so we accept $H_0$.
That is, the standard deviation of daily sales is equal to 10 units at the 0.05
level of significance.
:::

**2.4.2** The daily change in an exchange rate over `r e2_n` trading days has a
standard deviation of `r e2_s` baht. Assuming normality,
construct a 90% confidence interval for the standard deviation of the daily change.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 2.4.2"}
$(n-1)s^2 = `r e2_df`(`r num(e2_s^2)`) = `r num(e2_ss)`$;
$\chi^2_{0.05,\,`r e2_df`} = `r e2_lo_c`$, $\chi^2_{0.95,\,`r e2_df`} = `r e2_hi_c`$.
CI for $\sigma^2$: (`r fmt(e2_v_lo, 4)`, `r fmt(e2_v_hi, 4)`); CI for $\sigma$:
(`r fmt(sqrt(e2_v_lo), 4)`, `r fmt(sqrt(e2_v_hi), 4)`). We are 90% confident that
the standard deviation of the daily change is between `r fmt(sqrt(e2_v_lo), 4)`
and `r fmt(sqrt(e2_v_hi), 4)` baht.
:::

**2.4.3** Explain why the confidence interval for $\sigma^2$ is not of the form
"estimate $\pm$ margin of error".

::: {.answer title="Exercise 2.4.3"}
The chi-square distribution is skewed to the right, so the two critical values
are not the same distance from the centre. Dividing $(n-1)s^2$ by them gives
limits that are not equally far from $s^2$.
:::
